reasoning.counterfactual: Without perfusion/peritoneal concerns, a selected uncomplicated incarceration could receive supervised reduction assessment; an ordinary nonstrangulating obstruction would invoke a different pathway.
reasoning.deletion: Removing reduced enhancement/guarding makes reduction more credible. Stool passage earns its role as the closest-error trap, not as an empirical sensitivity claim.
reasoning.cueAttack: The record uses observations rather than 'strangulation.' All three options are urgent hospital management pathways, not elective clinics against a unique rescue key. No exact treatment interval is asserted.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard from distinguishing incarceration, ischemia and nonstrangulating obstruction pathways.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone; no earlier diagnosis answer gives the ischemia interpretation.
reasoning.stage: Initial hospital management before operative exploration, reviewed later in clinic.
reasoning.repair: New concept versions the narrower ischemia-response meaning; does not move old general elective-referral FSRS history.

definitions.name: Laura Bennett
definitions.presentation: Laura Bennett, a 39-year-old woman, attends clinic for difficulty bracing her trunk during exercise. Raising her shoulders produces broad midline doming. Examination and targeted ultrasound show an intact but widened linea alba, without a focal opening or hernia sac. She has no episodic focal pain.

nodes.objective: Use the intact widened linea alba and functional symptoms to select an initial nonoperative plan rather than hernia repair.
nodes.task: Which initial treatment plan best fits Laura Bennett's abdominal-wall findings?

choices.label: Refer for physiotherapy assessment
choices.rationale: The functional complaint accompanies diastasis without a focal hernia; physiotherapy may be tried before surgery.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes broad midline separation from a focal defect needing repair.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Arrange focal midline mesh hernia repair
choices.rationale: There is no focal opening or sac to support the proposed hernia operation.
choices.temptation: Treats every visible abdominal dome as a hernia.
choices.correctUnder: A separate symptomatic focal defect would justify hernia repair assessment.

choices.label: Schedule operative linea alba plication now
choices.rationale: Plication is an operative option, but bypassing an initial functional rehabilitation assessment is not the preferred first plan in this presentation.
choices.temptation: Confuses an available definitive operation with the initial treatment stage.
choices.correctUnder: Persistent troublesome diastasis after nonoperative management and an informed operative preference could justify plication discussion.

nodes.explanation: The widened but intact midline supports diastasis rather than a focal hernia. For Laura's core-function complaint, physiotherapy can precede surgical consideration. This recommendation does not specify one proven exercise protocol or require every patient to avoid surgery.

steps: Interpret intact widened fascia as diastasis rather than a hernia opening.
Match the functional complaint and initial stage to rehabilitation before operative correction.
reasoning.closestError: Schedule mesh hernia repair based on the dome alone.
reasoning.decider: No focal opening or sac is present, and this is the initial treatment assessment.
reasoning.counterfactual: A separate painful focal hernia would change the repair discussion; persistent symptoms after rehabilitation could justify plication assessment.
reasoning.deletion: The ultrasound establishes that the apparent ridge has no focal defect; functional impairment explains why simple reassurance is not the only plan. No exercise duration is fabricated.
reasoning.cueAttack: All answers are named treatments. Removed a diagnosis-repeating task and an absolute no-surgery answer. The task does not use 'core' as a key-only word.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate at the lower end; initial-stage versus immediate plication is the close error. Weak guideline ranking requires clinician confirmation.
reasoning.sequence: First node; feedback does not name the later coexisting-defect material recommendation.
reasoning.stage: Initial treatment of symptomatic diastasis.
reasoning.repair: Material objective change from recognition to treatment gets a new concept identity; original recognition history remains preserved. The negative focal-defect observation is clinically necessary, not removable cue padding.

nodes.objective: Choose a mesh-based repair strategy when a symptomatic focal hernia coexists with rectus diastasis.
nodes.task: Which repair strategy best fits Laura Bennett's new focal abdominal-wall problem?
nodes.update: At a later visit Laura's trunk endurance has improved. She now has a focal navel bulge that stops her lifting at work and reduces when she lies down. Ultrasound shows a 2.5-cm umbilical opening within the persistently widened linea alba. After counseling, she chooses elective repair.

choices.label: Mesh-reinforced repair of the umbilical hernia
choices.rationale: The symptomatic focal hernia is now a distinct problem within a widened midline; mesh-based repair is suggested rather than isolated suture repair.
choices.temptation: Uses the coexisting defect to change a previously reasonable rehabilitation-only interpretation.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Primary sutured repair of the umbilical hernia
choices.rationale: Associated diastasis makes treating the focal defect as an isolated suture problem less attractive because of recurrence concerns.
choices.temptation: Applies a small isolated-defect shortcut while ignoring the surrounding midline.
choices.correctUnder: An appropriately selected very small isolated defect without diastasis could allow a suture-repair discussion.

choices.label: Suture plication of the widened linea alba
choices.rationale: Plication aimed at the diastasis does not supply the supported mesh-based strategy for this symptomatic coexisting hernia.
choices.temptation: Treats the new focal symptoms as persistence of the original diffuse problem.
choices.correctUnder: Diastasis without a concomitant hernia can be considered for plication after appropriate counseling.

nodes.explanation: The new focal opening changes the operative question. Improvement in endurance does not remove a symptomatic hernia within the widened linea alba. Mesh-based hernia repair is suggested; whether to correct the entire diastasis simultaneously remains a separate decision.

steps: Recognize a new focal hernia coexisting with the original diastasis rather than failure of trunk rehabilitation.
Apply the coexisting-diastasis repair boundary to choose mesh-based reinforcement.
reasoning.closestError: Use an isolated small-defect suture repair or diastasis plication for the combined problem.
reasoning.decider: A focal 2.5-cm symptomatic opening exists within the widened linea alba and repair has been chosen.
reasoning.counterfactual: If the linea alba were widened but intact, isolated diastasis treatment could be considered; a very small isolated defect without diastasis would change the suture discussion.
reasoning.deletion: The new ultrasound finding and the background widened midline both matter. Without the new focal defect, the preceding rehabilitation interpretation would persist.
reasoning.cueAttack: All options are reconstruction strategies at the same phase. Shared hernia closure is balanced between key and nearest competitor; no generic individualized plan or unique multiple-component key.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard; the temptation is a familiar isolated-defect repair applied to a different abdominal-wall substrate.
reasoning.sequence: Earlier feedback supports rehabilitation only for intact fascia. It does not state mesh use for a later focal defect. Newly returned anatomy changes the decision.
reasoning.stage: Elective repair strategy after the decision to operate, not initial diagnosis or urgency.
reasoning.repair: New coverage of a consequential coexisting-defect boundary; the 2.5-cm observation is fictional patient anatomy, not a newly invented treatment cutoff.

definitions.name: Owen Hayes
definitions.presentation: Owen Hayes, a 66-year-old man, attends clinic with a recurrent bulge after two midline incisional repairs. Standing examination identifies more than one reducible protrusion across a long scar. The old operative reports describe different implant planes, but their diagrams do not show how the meshes overlap. He wants repair because the bulges prevent bending at work.

nodes.objective: Distinguish confirmation of a palpable hernia from the additional anatomical mapping needed before recurrent repair.
nodes.task: Which investigation should guide Owen Hayes's recurrent repair planning?

choices.label: Computed tomography for abdominal-wall mapping
choices.rationale: Cross-sectional mapping can show the full defect, prior mesh relationships and abdominal contents before a complex recurrent repair.
choices.temptation: Recognizes that proving one palpable opening does not map the repair.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Targeted ultrasound of the largest palpable opening
choices.rationale: It can verify that opening but does not provide the needed whole-wall map of multiple recurrences and old implants.
choices.temptation: Confuses diagnostic confirmation with preoperative planning.
choices.correctUnder: An isolated small equivocal defect without complex prior repairs could be assessed with targeted ultrasound.

choices.label: Diagnostic laparoscopy to survey the old repair
choices.rationale: An invasive survey is not the preferred initial mapping step for this elective recurrent defect.
choices.temptation: Uses operative inspection to replace available preoperative anatomical planning.
choices.correctUnder: A selected persistently symptomatic occult defect after nondiagnostic noninvasive evaluation may justify diagnostic laparoscopy.

nodes.explanation: The diagnosis is already evident. The unanswered question is the full recurrent defect and old-mesh anatomy needed to plan repair. Cross-sectional imaging addresses that question before an invasive survey.

steps: Recognize that examination confirms recurrence but leaves its full anatomy and implant relationships unresolved.
Choose cross-sectional planning instead of a narrow confirmatory study or an initial invasive survey.
reasoning.closestError: Obtain only an ultrasound of the largest bulge because a hernia is suspected.
reasoning.decider: Multiple recurrences and conflicting prior plane records require a whole-wall map.
reasoning.counterfactual: One tiny intermittent defect without previous implants could make targeted dynamic ultrasound a suitable first investigation.
reasoning.deletion: Without multiple prior repairs and unresolved implant relationships, ultrasound becomes a stronger competitor. Actual work limitation explains why operative planning is being pursued.
reasoning.cueAttack: No sentence names CT or declares that ultrasound is inadequate. Three actual investigations have equal wait metadata; the invasive option is a credible selected-case route, with its limits explained after answering.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard from diagnostic-versus-planning scope; modality sophistication alone does not create difficulty.
reasoning.sequence: First node; feedback does not supply a defect-width threshold or dictate a release. New CT anatomy drives the next decision.
reasoning.stage: Preoperative investigation before selecting the reconstructive venue and expertise.
reasoning.repair: New coverage of recurrent repair planning, rather than another plane-name question.

nodes.objective: Use wide recurrent anatomy to recognize the limits of a routine closable-defect repair pathway without claiming CT proves a specific release.
nodes.task: Which planning decision best fits Owen Hayes's returned CT findings?
nodes.update: CT shows a 12-cm transverse recurrent fascial opening with retracted lateral muscle complexes and several adjacent defects. Much of the bowel lies in the chronic sac. The proposed local service performs routine closable incisional repairs but does not perform myofascial releases.

choices.label: Refer for hospital abdominal-wall reconstruction planning
choices.rationale: The anatomy raises a realistic need for release expertise and loss-of-domain planning beyond a routine closable-defect service.
choices.temptation: Applies the limit of the elective guideline rather than promising a particular operation from CT.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Book routine local fascial closure with mesh reinforcement
choices.rationale: The returned anatomy does not support assuming a straightforward closure within this service's scope.
choices.temptation: Extends a feasible-closure recommendation to a wide recurrent defect.
choices.correctUnder: A smaller uncomplicated defect expected to close without release could fit routine local repair.

choices.label: Book local mesh bridging without further reconstruction review
choices.rationale: A bridge should not become the default response to suspected closure difficulty before specialist reconstructive planning.
choices.temptation: Substitutes bridging for assessing how function might be restored.
choices.correctUnder: A salvage situation after expert evaluation may require a bridge; that is not established by this elective CT alone.

nodes.explanation: CT suggests complexity; it does not prove that a particular release or adjunct must be used. A wide recurrent defect with retracted muscles should be planned by a team with reconstructive expertise. The ordinary closable-defect recommendation does not justify forceful closure or default bridging.

steps: Interpret the width, retraction and chronic sac as a complex repair rather than a routine closable defect.
Match that uncertainty and likely expertise requirement to specialist planning rather than preselecting a local operation.
reasoning.closestError: Apply 'close the fascia and reinforce' without checking whether that is feasible in the proposed service.
reasoning.decider: Wide recurrent anatomy with retraction and a service limited to routine repairs.
reasoning.counterfactual: An uncomplicated smaller defect expected to approximate without release would support routine fascial closure and mesh reinforcement.
reasoning.deletion: Removing the CT loses the reason to leave routine scope. The service limitation is a real capability constraint, not a permission sentence announcing that a keyed test is available.
reasoning.cueAttack: Removed 'closure is feasible' and 'closure requires TAR' author conclusions. The task asks for planning, and each option specifies a venue/repair pathway. No high-tension distractor caricature or automatic CT-to-TAR rule.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted hard; the error is applying a correct narrow guideline to the wrong reconstruction scope.
reasoning.sequence: The preceding CT rationale does not name the advanced referral. Returned width and muscle/sac findings are necessary; deleting them restores a routine plan as a reasonable competitor.
reasoning.stage: Reconstructive planning after imaging, not an intraoperative layer-closure question.
reasoning.repair: New concept versions the complexity/referral meaning. The old fascial-closure concept and its parked basic item are preserved, not relabelled moderate.

definitions.name: Victor Reed
definitions.presentation: Victor Reed, a 61-year-old man, attends clinic to review his hospital plan for elective midline incisional repair. The fascial edges are expected to approximate without advanced release. The proposed dissection can create a pocket behind rectus with an intact posterior sheath between the implant and bowel. There is no active infection or acute bowel event.

nodes.objective: Select an elective retromuscular reinforcement plan from anatomical boundaries and guideline scope rather than merely naming a compartment.
nodes.task: Which reinforcement plan best fits Victor Reed's documented elective repair?

choices.label: Fascial closure with retrorectus mesh reinforcement
choices.rationale: The described pocket is retrorectus, and retromuscular reinforcement is the preferred elective midline plan within this scope.
choices.temptation: Combines anatomical interpretation with selection of the reinforcement plane.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Fascial closure with subcutaneous onlay mesh reinforcement
choices.rationale: Onlay is an alternative, but the available retromuscular pocket fits the preferred elective recommendation.
choices.temptation: Extends the emergency onlay preference to a straightforward elective repair.
choices.correctUnder: An emergency repair selected for mesh, or an unavailable deep pocket, could change the plane discussion.

choices.label: Fascial closure with intraperitoneal mesh reinforcement
choices.rationale: This would expose the implant to a different compartment despite an available extra-abdominal-content pocket; visceral exposure merits caution.
choices.temptation: Assumes all mesh deep to the abdominal wall has the same implications.
choices.correctUnder: When extraperitoneal placement is not feasible, an appropriate intraperitoneal implant may be considered after technique-specific assessment.

nodes.explanation: Behind rectus and in front of posterior sheath is retrorectus, part of the retromuscular space. Use that interpretation to select the elective guideline-supported plane. This preference has low-certainty evidence and does not settle emergency or technically unavailable-plane cases.

steps: Locate the pocket relative to muscle, sheath and bowel.
Apply elective rather than emergency guidance to select reinforcement within that compartment.
reasoning.closestError: Choose onlay by importing an emergency recommendation, or assume every deep plane is intraperitoneal.
reasoning.decider: Elective closable midline scope plus an available intact retrorectus pocket.
reasoning.counterfactual: In an acute emergency case with a chosen mesh repair, the 2026 EHS plane recommendation differs; no universal plane ranking is carried between those settings.
reasoning.deletion: Both the anatomy and elective scope are required. Without a usable pocket, intraperitoneal/onlay alternatives deserve a different discussion.
reasoning.cueAttack: All options contain the same fascial closure and differ in plane only. Necessary anatomical boundaries replace the plane label in the presentation. The key is not a unique comprehensive plan; no 2x2 majority-component construction.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate; anatomy plus care-phase scope are consequential. The original four label-recall versions were much easier.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone; no previous explanation has named the space.
reasoning.stage: Elective reinforcement plan after closure feasibility is established.
reasoning.repair: New clinical meaning gets a new concept ID; the old plane-recognition identity is retained for historical encounters.

definitions.name: Grace Allen
definitions.presentation: Grace Allen, a 63-year-old woman, attends clinic for a reducible incisional hernia that limits gardening. The bulge softens when she lies down and she is eating normally. She also has COPD; she now becomes breathless walking across the room and uses her rescue inhaler more often than before. Her examination shows diffuse expiratory wheezing rather than focal hernia tenderness.

nodes.objective: Use the current respiratory and hernia findings to distinguish modifiable elective readiness from an acute hernia indication.
nodes.task: Which step should guide Grace Allen's elective hernia scheduling now?

choices.label: Arrange respiratory reassessment before elective scheduling
choices.rationale: The symptomatic hernia merits planning, but the current respiratory deterioration is a modifiable elective risk that needs assessment.
choices.temptation: Does not let a legitimate repair indication substitute for operative readiness.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Arrange elective scheduling using current respiratory treatment
choices.rationale: The new breathlessness, escalating rescue use and wheeze need reassessment before final elective scheduling.
choices.temptation: Confuses a stable reducible hernia with a patient already ready for surgery.
choices.correctUnder: Stable optimized respiratory status and completed risk assessment could support scheduling.

choices.label: Transfer for emergency hernia exploration during this visit
choices.rationale: The hernia itself reduces and has no acute obstructive or persistent local findings; respiratory assessment is a separate need.
choices.temptation: Treats respiratory symptoms as evidence that the hernia has strangulated.
choices.correctUnder: New nonreducibility with vomiting or guarding would change the hernia pathway.

nodes.explanation: Grace's hernia symptoms justify continued elective planning, but her new respiratory findings require assessment and optimization before fixing a date. The hernia's reducibility does not establish pulmonary readiness. Respiratory care may itself require escalation based on assessment; no drug regimen or fixed delay is prescribed here.

steps: Attribute the new readiness problem to the respiratory course while confirming that the hernia remains reducible and nonobstructed.
Address modifiable pulmonary risk before final elective scheduling without permanently excluding repair.
reasoning.closestError: Schedule because reducibility establishes that the case is elective.
reasoning.decider: New room-crossing breathlessness, greater rescue use and wheeze despite a reducible nontender hernia.
reasoning.counterfactual: If her pulmonary status were stable and optimized, an elective date could be finalized; acute hernia changes would instead override routine optimization.
reasoning.deletion: Both trajectories are needed to distinguish indication, readiness and urgency. No exact pulmonary target or mandatory number of weeks is invented.
reasoning.cueAttack: Removed the diagnostic label 'poorly controlled COPD' as the deciding observation; actual course is supplied. Three scheduling pathways are concrete. The key is not a vague general optimization phrase beside absurd permanent contraindication options.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate at the lower end; the main error is conflating elective classification with readiness. New variant does not inherit the older approval or tutorial exception.
reasoning.sequence: First node; feedback does not teach an indefinite weight-loss policy.
reasoning.stage: Elective readiness assessment, not a particular COPD regimen or anesthetic technique.
reasoning.repair: Additional application variant of the exact approved pulmonary concept; neither approved original is replaced or reapproved.

nodes.objective: Balance persistent operative risk against the consequences of indefinite delay after a genuine pre-optimization effort.
nodes.task: Which plan should now guide Grace Allen's hernia care after pre-optimization?
nodes.update: At later review her respiratory symptoms have returned to baseline after treatment, and she stopped smoking. She completed a supervised weight-loss programme without sustained weight reduction. The hernia remains reducible but has enlarged, and pain now stops household tasks. Cross-sectional planning suggests repair is technically possible. She wants to reconsider surgery after discussing the risks.

choices.label: Proceed with elective hernia repair scheduling
choices.rationale: After a dedicated unsuccessful weight-loss effort, worsening function and enlargement can shift the balance toward repair planning.
choices.temptation: Balances the harms of delay against persistent operative risk rather than imposing an invented threshold.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Defer elective hernia repair for further weight loss
choices.rationale: Further delay has real symptom and defect costs; there is no supported universal target supplied that must be reached first.
choices.temptation: Turns a modifiable risk factor into an indefinite prerequisite.
choices.correctUnder: An incomplete optimization attempt with tolerable symptoms could favor more prehabilitation before scheduling.

choices.label: Defer elective hernia repair until after bariatric surgery
choices.rationale: Bariatric-first treatment may suit selected patients, but the record does not establish it as a required prerequisite despite worsening symptoms.
choices.temptation: Substitutes one universal sequence for individualized risk-benefit assessment.
choices.correctUnder: Appropriate bariatric eligibility, patient goals and a tolerable hernia could justify a coordinated bariatric-first strategy.

nodes.explanation: Optimization is not a rule to delay every symptomatic repair indefinitely. Grace completed a genuine effort, other risks improved, and the hernia is enlarging with worsening function. Those observations support a new repair discussion while preserving explicit counseling about the remaining weight-associated risks.

steps: Distinguish a completed unsuccessful effort from an unattempted optimization programme.
Balance worsening symptoms and enlargement against remaining operative risk to reopen repair planning.
reasoning.closestError: Keep deferring until an arbitrary target weight is reached.
reasoning.decider: A documented effort plus worsening function and technically feasible repair.
reasoning.counterfactual: If the programme had not been attempted and symptoms remained tolerable, further optimization could reasonably precede scheduling.
reasoning.deletion: Removing the completed programme makes continued optimization more defensible; removing worsening function weakens the cost-of-delay argument. No BMI cutoff is supplied or implied.
reasoning.cueAttack: All three options are named sequencing policies. The key states a concrete next stage, not 'individualize care.' No uniquely cautious omnibus plan or invented target numerical weight.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard from two legitimate competing risks; guideline is a good-practice statement, so exact eligibility needs clinician review.
reasoning.sequence: Earlier pulmonary recommendation required action on an active modifiable problem. The returned actual response and completed weight effort change the remaining decision; the prior answer cannot settle it.
reasoning.stage: Elective sequencing after a completed pre-optimization interval.
reasoning.repair: New gap coverage; no original approved pulmonary version or history is modified.

definitions.name: Sofia Lane
definitions.presentation: Sofia Lane, a 31-year-old woman, attends clinic with a small navel hernia that reduces freely. It causes little discomfort and does not limit activity. She plans another pregnancy and asks about arranging repair first. The skin is intact and bowel function is normal.

nodes.objective: Use planned future pregnancy to alter the timing of otherwise elective primary hernia repair.
nodes.task: Which timing plan best fits Sofia Lane's current hernia and pregnancy plans?

choices.label: Defer repair until after the last planned pregnancy
choices.rationale: The hernia is reducible and tolerable, and a later pregnancy increases recurrence risk after repair.
choices.temptation: Separates the fact that elective repair is possible from the best timing for her current goals.
choices.correctUnder: Current case, with reassessment if symptoms change.

choices.label: Complete elective mesh repair before the next pregnancy
choices.rationale: Repair now does not remove the recurrence implications of the planned pregnancy; deferral is reasonable when symptoms allow.
choices.temptation: Treats stronger reinforcement as a way to eliminate the timing tradeoff.
choices.correctUnder: Inability to defer because of significant symptoms would require a specific pre-pregnancy repair discussion.

choices.label: Complete elective suture repair before the next pregnancy
choices.rationale: Changing material does not make immediate repair preferable in this currently tolerable presentation.
choices.temptation: Assumes avoiding mesh resolves all reasons to defer.
choices.correctUnder: When repair cannot be postponed, suture versus mesh is a separate weak-evidence discussion requiring exact clinical sign-off.

nodes.explanation: Sofia's reducible, tolerable hernia permits deferral. Subsequent pregnancy can increase recurrence after repair, so the timing discussion differs from that for someone who has completed childbearing. If symptoms become unacceptable, the case needs reassessment; no universal pre-pregnancy mesh-versus-suture rule is scored.

steps: Establish that the current hernia does not force urgent or symptom-driven immediate repair.
Apply the planned-pregnancy recurrence consideration to defer the elective operation.
reasoning.closestError: Recommend mesh now on the assumption that material removes the pregnancy-related recurrence issue.
reasoning.decider: Another pregnancy is planned and symptoms allow postponement.
reasoning.counterfactual: Completed childbearing with persistent work-limiting symptoms would favor elective repair planning rather than this pregnancy-specific deferral.
reasoning.deletion: Removing the pregnancy plan eliminates the timing reason; removing reducibility and tolerable symptoms would make deferral unsafe or unacceptable.
reasoning.cueAttack: All options are definite timing/repair plans. No 'shared decision' answer or unsupported numerical recurrence estimate. Pregnancy is clinically necessary, not decorative preference cueing.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate from an otherwise reasonable pre-pregnancy repair competitor; exact timing recommendation is weak evidence and remains for clinician review.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone; no prior explanation supplies pregnancy advice.
reasoning.stage: Elective operation timing, not an obstetric management or emergency pathway.
reasoning.repair: New topic gap with a constrained pregnancy-capable profile; no random sex or age recombination is supplied.

definitions.name: Martin Cole
definitions.presentation: Martin Cole, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic after discharge while the founder reviews his emergency incisional-hernia operation. At the end of the recorded operation the bowel injury had been resected, the remaining bowel was pink and contracting, and repeated inspection showed no continuing leak. He no longer required escalating circulatory support. During gentle approximation the fascial edges remained far apart, but the sac and skin could cover the abdominal contents without tension.

nodes.objective: Distinguish deferral of definitive fascial reconstruction from an indication to leave a stable source-controlled abdomen open.
nodes.task: Which closure strategy best fits Martin Cole's recorded end-of-operation findings?

choices.label: Close the abdominal cavity with sac and skin; defer wall repair
choices.rationale: Stable physiology, source control and no second-look need support closing the cavity while deferring complex reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Separates abdominal-cavity closure from definitive restoration of the fascial wall.
choices.correctUnder: Current recorded phase.

choices.label: Close the abdominal cavity with advanced release and mesh repair
choices.rationale: The emergency guidance favors deferring advanced reconstruction when direct closure is not possible.
choices.temptation: Imports elective reconstruction goals into the emergency source-control operation.
choices.correctUnder: A later optimized elective reconstruction with appropriate expertise may use a release technique.

choices.label: Cover the abdominal cavity with a temporary dressing for re-exploration
choices.rationale: The record supplies no ongoing physiology, bowel-reassessment or compartment reason to leave the cavity open.
choices.temptation: Equates inability to close fascia with a mandatory open abdomen.
choices.correctUnder: Continuing resuscitation, uncertain bowel viability or pressure-related organ dysfunction could justify temporary open closure.

nodes.explanation: A fascial gap and an open abdomen are different problems. In this stable source-controlled phase, the cavity can be closed using available tissues and the definitive reconstruction deferred. This 2026 conditional recommendation does not apply when bowel reassessment or ongoing physiological derangement still requires an open abdomen.

steps: Separate the unclosable fascial defect from the available safe cavity covering and absence of a second-look indication.
Choose cavity closure with deferred reconstruction instead of immediate advanced release or unnecessary open-abdomen management.
reasoning.closestError: Leave every unclosable fascial defect as an open abdomen.
reasoning.decider: Source-controlled viable bowel, settled support and tension-free sac/skin coverage despite a persistent fascial gap.
reasoning.counterfactual: A dusky segment requiring reassessment or worsening physiology during closure would favor temporary closure and a second look, matching the separate frozen N2 meaning.
reasoning.deletion: Removing bowel/support reassessment data makes temporary closure plausible. Removing the available covering makes the proposed cavity closure unsupported. These negatives establish real eligibility rather than merely eliminate option names.
reasoning.cueAttack: No 'stable source control complete' shorthand is used in the vignette; observable findings establish it. Three real end-of-operation strategies have comparable scope. The key does not claim definitive repair or introduce an unavailable ICU at the clinic.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted hard because an appropriate open-abdomen principle becomes wrong when applied solely to the fascial gap. Very-low-certainty current guidance requires explicit clinical review.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone chart review. Frozen N2 wording/feedback is not altered and not inserted as a companion.
reasoning.stage: End of an outside emergency operation, not an actual clinic operation.
reasoning.repair: New gap separates cavity versus wall closure and preserves the old temporary-closure construct.

definitions.name: Thomas Avery
definitions.presentation: Thomas Avery, a 60-year-old man, attends clinic after discharge while the founder reviews an outside emergency ventral-hernia repair. The trapped bowel recovered after release. A small opening was repaired; the field was dry on repeated inspection after a limited spill was suctioned. His physiology remained unchanged. The fascia met with gentle approximation; a closed posterior layer separated the planned mesh-based repair from bowel.

nodes.objective: Apply the selected controlled-contamination material rule without extending it to uncontrolled leakage or all emergency reconstructions.
nodes.task: Which implant material best fits Thomas Avery's selected mesh-based repair?

choices.label: Permanent macroporous polypropylene mesh
choices.rationale: The controlled bowel event in this stable selected repair does not require abandoning permanent macroporous synthetic reinforcement.
choices.temptation: Avoids automatic biologic substitution after any bowel entry.
choices.correctUnder: Current selected repair scope.

choices.label: Non-cross-linked porcine dermal tissue matrix
choices.rationale: A biologic implant is not automatically preferred solely because this controlled bowel opening occurred.
choices.temptation: Applies an older contamination slogan without checking source control and selection.
choices.correctUnder: A different reconstructive context could justify a biologic discussion, but no universal alternative indication is asserted here.

choices.label: Permanent microporous expanded polytetrafluoroethylene
choices.rationale: Current emergency guidance favors permanent macroporous synthetic material rather than this microporous alternative in the selected scope.
choices.temptation: Treats all permanent synthetic implants as equivalent.
choices.correctUnder: A different clean, technique-specific reconstruction could require another implant assessment; this packet does not prescribe ePTFE for a contaminated visceral-contact case.

nodes.explanation: First establish the selected scope from the repaired bowel, controlled contamination, unchanged physiology and direct closure. Then choose the supported macroporous synthetic material. The answer does not decide repair timing after uncontrolled leakage, nor does it turn the elective plane preference into an emergency rule.

steps: Infer the selected controlled-contamination scope from operative observations.
Choose macroporous permanent synthetic material rather than treating bowel entry as an automatic biologic indication.
reasoning.closestError: Choose biologic material because the bowel was entered, or equate all synthetic pore constructions.
reasoning.decider: A repaired limited bowel event, no continuing leak and a selected closable mesh repair separate this case from an unresolved contamination problem.
reasoning.counterfactual: Persistent leakage, uncertain bowel viability or inability to directly close would invalidate the selected material question and require a different closure/reconstruction decision, not an automatic alternative polymer.
reasoning.deletion: Each operative observation defines the selection boundary. Removing the repaired/dry-field data makes the question prematurely ask for a material.
reasoning.cueAttack: Three concrete implant materials, no 'solely because' or 'regardless' distractor labels. No answer rationale appears in the record. The key shares material specificity with competitors and is not a uniquely complete plan.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate; a transfer variant of a represented rule, not a new meaning or a new independent trial. No approval inherited from row 044.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone. Exact N1/N4 accepted variants remain frozen and are not combined into a repetitive scored sequence.
reasoning.stage: Material selection after deciding on a selected mesh-based repair.
reasoning.repair: Additional question on an existing approved meaning, with new exact unapproved wording and a clinic record-review frame.

definitions.name: Erin Walsh
definitions.presentation: Erin Walsh, a 56-year-old woman, attends clinic after laparoscopic ventral mesh repair. A soft fullness is visible at the old sac. It is painless, the incision is dry and healed, and she is eating and walking normally. The hospital scan shows a simple fluid pocket at the sac, an intact repair and no recurrent fascial opening.

nodes.objective: Separate a postoperative fluid pocket from recurrence and use symptom burden to avoid unnecessary intervention.
nodes.task: Which plan best fits Erin Walsh's current postoperative fullness?

choices.label: Observe the fluid pocket with clinical follow-up
choices.rationale: The intact repair and painless simple pocket support an asymptomatic seroma pathway.
choices.temptation: Does not treat the presence of fluid alone as recurrence or infection.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Perform sterile needle aspiration of the fluid pocket
choices.rationale: The pocket is not symptomatic; aspiration is not required simply because it is visible.
choices.temptation: Treats every postoperative collection as needing drainage.
choices.correctUnder: A persistent symptomatic seroma could justify sterile drainage assessment.

choices.label: Schedule operative revision of the hernia reconstruction
choices.rationale: The scan shows no recurrent opening and symptoms do not suggest a structural repair failure.
choices.temptation: Equates postoperative contour fullness with recurrence.
choices.correctUnder: A demonstrated recurrent fascial defect with troublesome symptoms could require repair planning.

nodes.explanation: Interpret what forms the fullness before treating it. An intact repair with a painless simple fluid pocket supports observation. A visible pocket does not by itself require aspiration or a new hernia operation.

steps: Use the completed scan to separate a fluid pocket from a recurrent defect.
Use its lack of symptoms to choose observation rather than procedural treatment.
reasoning.closestError: Aspirate because a collection exists, or revise because a bulge exists.
reasoning.decider: Intact fascial repair plus a painless simple pocket and normal recovery.
reasoning.counterfactual: A persistent pocket causing functional pain would justify drainage assessment; a recurrent fascial opening would change the structural repair discussion.
reasoning.deletion: Without the intact-repair finding, revision is more credible. Without the symptom course, aspiration versus observation cannot be ranked fairly.
reasoning.cueAttack: No seroma label appears before answering. All options are management plans; aspiration receives its own wait metadata. The observation option includes the same follow-up scope rather than a uniquely elaborate safety plan.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate at the lower end; an unnecessary intervention is a real clinical error, not a basic exception claim.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone initial-assessment variant. No subsequent update or sibling feedback is visible.
reasoning.stage: Initial outpatient management after completed imaging.
reasoning.repair: New postoperative-complication gap; no arbitrary postoperative duration or aspiration frequency.

definitions.name: Erin Walsh
definitions.presentation: Erin Walsh, a 56-year-old woman, attends clinic after laparoscopic ventral mesh repair. A soft fullness is visible at the old sac. It is painless, the incision is dry and healed, and she is eating and walking normally. The hospital scan shows a simple fluid pocket at the sac, an intact repair and no recurrent fascial opening.

nodes.objective: Reassess a previously observed seroma when persistent mechanical symptoms emerge without evidence of infection or recurrence.
nodes.task: Which next plan best fits Erin Walsh's changed postoperative fluid pocket?
nodes.update: At later review the pocket persists and pressure over it now makes bending painful. Repeat imaging again shows the same simple fluid pocket and an intact repair. The wound remains healed; there is no fever, erythema or deep tract.

choices.label: Arrange sterile image-guided aspiration assessment
choices.rationale: Persistent function-limiting symptoms can justify drainage assessment of an otherwise uncomplicated seroma.
choices.temptation: Changes management because of the actual symptom trajectory, not simply persistence on a calendar.
choices.correctUnder: Current case.

choices.label: Continue observation at the previous review interval
choices.rationale: The prior painless course has changed to a persistent function-limiting complaint.
choices.temptation: Anchors on the earlier benign interpretation and overlooks the new treatment indication.
choices.correctUnder: A painless pocket not affecting function could continue to be observed.

choices.label: Plan complete mesh excision and operative debridement
choices.rationale: The record lacks a deep infectious focus or failed infection salvage to justify implant excision.
choices.temptation: Equates persistent fluid with prosthetic infection.
choices.correctUnder: Confirmed persistent deep implant infection after adequate source control could justify excision planning.

nodes.explanation: The structural and infectious assessments remain reassuring, but the symptom burden has changed. A persistent painful seroma can be considered for sterile drainage. Persistence alone is not proof of infection and does not justify mesh removal.

steps: Maintain the fluid-pocket interpretation while excluding a newly demonstrated recurrence or infection from the supplied observations.
Use actual new functional pain to move from observation to sterile drainage assessment.
reasoning.closestError: Continue the old observation plan solely because the scan still looks benign.
reasoning.decider: The same pocket now causes persistent bending pain with intact repair and no infectious trajectory.
reasoning.counterfactual: If it remained painless, observation would still fit; if a deep infected tract developed, source-control planning would replace simple seroma management.
reasoning.deletion: Removing the new bending limitation returns the earlier observation key. The unchanged scan is necessary to distinguish a symptom-driven intervention from structural failure.
reasoning.cueAttack: No calendar trigger or 'needs drainage' phrase supplied. Specific actions at the same follow-up stage; aspiration has a wait preview, and other choices have explicit no-test classifications.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate from trajectory versus static-image reasoning; low-certainty procedural ranking needs clinician confirmation.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone follow-up variant. Earlier history is supplied as case context; no earlier scored answer or feedback is visible. The current update must change the decision from the earlier observation pathway.
reasoning.stage: Follow-up procedural management after reassessment.
reasoning.repair: A second variant of the same narrow seroma concept, not a second invented learning meaning.

definitions.name: Peter Shaw
definitions.presentation: Peter Shaw, a 59-year-old man, attends clinic while the founder reviews the closure record from an elective midline laparotomy. The aponeurotic edges were healthy and came together without force. The first closure used wide, widely spaced bites incorporating muscle; the log records 18 cm of suture consumed over a 12-cm wound. The surgeon paused before completing the closure.

nodes.objective: Recognize a technically deficient elective closure from tissue acquisition and suture consumption, then select the supported repair of the technique.
nodes.task: Which closure plan best addresses Peter Shaw's recorded findings?

choices.label: Replace the closure with a small-bites suture line
choices.rationale: Re-suture using low-tension aponeurotic bites, slowly absorbable material and adequate suture consumption. This addresses the recorded acquisition and 1.5:1 ratio.
choices.temptation: Corrects the demonstrated primary closure problem rather than covering it with reinforcement.
choices.correctUnder: Current elective healthy-edge scope.

choices.label: Retain the closure without mesh augmentation
choices.rationale: Easy edge apposition does not correct sparse muscle-containing bites and inadequate suture consumption.
choices.temptation: Accepts an apparently closed wound without checking how it was closed.
choices.correctUnder: A technically adequate low-tension small-bites closure in an appropriate lower-risk elective case could be retained without augmentation.

choices.label: Retain the closure and add onlay mesh augmentation
choices.rationale: Augmentation may be considered for selected elective laparotomies, but it does not repair the documented deficient primary technique.
choices.temptation: Uses reinforcement as a substitute for correcting a poor primary closure.
choices.correctUnder: A technically sound elective midline closure in a selected patient at higher hernia risk could receive prophylactic onlay augmentation after counseling.

nodes.explanation: The record shows sparse muscle-containing bites and a constructed suture-to-wound ratio of 18/12 = 1.5. The guideline's supported elective small-bites technique uses aponeurosis, slowly absorbable suture, low tension and a ratio of at least 4:1. No emergency closure rule is inferred from this elective recommendation.

steps: Interpret the acquired tissues and suture consumption as a closure-technique problem despite edges meeting easily.
Correct the primary suture line rather than merely accept or augment it.
reasoning.closestError: Add prophylactic mesh to compensate for a technically poor primary closure.
reasoning.decider: Sparse muscle-containing bites and 18 cm consumed over a 12-cm wound.
reasoning.counterfactual: With an already sound low-tension small-bites closure and adequate consumption, retaining the line would be appropriate; selected higher-risk elective cases could then consider augmentation.
reasoning.deletion: Without tissue capture and suture consumption the task becomes unsupported technique preference; without healthy approximating edges it could be a tension/release problem.
reasoning.cueAttack: Replaced two intrinsically poor technique distractors with real accept-versus-augment plans, both reasonable after a sound closure. Each label names the current suture-line action and has comparable length. The majority repeated component is 'retain,' which cannot assemble the key. Feedback holds the numerical rule; the record contains constructed observations.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard from recognizing why apparent easy apposition or reinforcement does not validate a deficient primary closure.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone. No prior feedback gives the 4:1 criterion before answering.
reasoning.stage: Final primary-closure plan during an outside elective operation, reviewed in clinic.
reasoning.repair: Manual gate repeated after replacing unsupported technique counterfactuals with two legitimate post-closure decisions; direct ratio and augmentation claims added.

definitions.name: Claire Hudson
definitions.presentation: Claire Hudson, a 52-year-old woman, attends clinic while the founder reviews her laparoscopic operation. A 5-mm umbilical port was enlarged to remove the specimen. The final operative measurement records a 12-mm fascial opening; the other lateral ports remained 5 mm. The layers are healthy and the specimen extraction is complete.

nodes.objective: Apply trocar-site closure guidance to the final fascial defect rather than the original trocar diameter.
nodes.task: How should Claire Hudson's enlarged umbilical fascial site be managed before routine skin closure?

choices.label: Suture the umbilical fascial opening
choices.rationale: The final defect is at least 10 mm and is umbilical, despite starting with a small trocar.
choices.temptation: Uses the acquired final anatomy rather than the original instrument label.
choices.correctUnder: Current final 12-mm umbilical opening.

choices.label: Leave the umbilical fascial opening unsutured
choices.rationale: The original 5-mm designation no longer describes the extraction defect.
choices.temptation: Carries forward an initial small-port plan after enlargement.
choices.correctUnder: An unchanged small port without enlargement or other risk considerations could have a different closure discussion.

choices.label: Suture the umbilical fascial opening and add onlay mesh
choices.rationale: The trocar guideline supports suturing this defect; it does not establish routine prophylactic onlay augmentation for this port.
choices.temptation: Imports prophylactic mesh guidance for adult laparotomy into a port-site decision.
choices.correctUnder: Selected elective midline laparotomy prophylaxis is a separate guideline question where augmentation after fascial closure may be considered.

nodes.explanation: Follow the final defect, not the initial port label. The 12-mm umbilical opening meets the guideline's suggested fascial-closure scope. Evidence is very low certainty and no optimal port suture material is established here.

steps: Recognize that specimen extraction changed the relevant fascial diameter from the original port size.
Apply the adult umbilical defect closure recommendation to the final opening.
reasoning.closestError: Close only skin because the instrument list says 5 mm.
reasoning.decider: The actual final umbilical fascial opening measures 12 mm.
reasoning.counterfactual: An unchanged small lateral port would not meet this same diameter/location indication.
reasoning.deletion: Removing the enlargement/final measurement leaves the original small-port plan defensible. Other port sizes distinguish the changed site from a blanket all-port policy.
reasoning.cueAttack: Task names the site, not the 10-mm rule. Every option is a closure plan, with no word 'alone' or explanatory wrong-answer qualifier. Original and final dimensions are fictional observed anatomy; the criterion is supported explicitly.
reasoning.difficulty: Predicted moderate at the lower end; the trap is provenance of the measurement rather than memorizing a port label. Independent difficulty review remains necessary.
reasoning.sequence: Standalone; no earlier laparotomy-closure feedback is exposed here.
reasoning.stage: Final closure after specimen extraction in an outside operative record.
reasoning.repair: New prevention gap; no invented mesh rule, wait duration or port-specific suture protocol.

questions.stem: Which plan should Maya Bennett follow for her current navel bulge?

answerChoices.label: Observe with scheduled reassessment and return precautions
answerChoices.rationale: The current symptom burden and preference permit observation; reassessment preserves the option to repair if the burden changes.

answerChoices.label: Arrange elective mesh repair at the next operative visit
answerChoices.rationale: Elective repair is an option but scheduling it now overrides her expressed preference despite limited impairment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Elective repair is an option but scheduling it now overrides her expressed preference despite limited impairment.

answerChoices.label: Arrange hospital exploration during the current visit
answerChoices.rationale: The bulge reduces and there are no acute obstructive or persistent local findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The bulge reduces and there are no acute obstructive or persistent local findings.

questions.explanation: Interpret reducibility and symptom impact separately. Maya's present burden and preference support observation with review and clear acute return precautions. Repair remains an option if the balance changes.

questions.stem: Which plan should now replace Maya Bennett's observation pathway?

answerChoices.label: Refer for elective abdominal-wall repair planning
answerChoices.rationale: New work interruption, local symptom concordance and changed preference alter the observation balance without establishing an emergency.

answerChoices.label: Continue observation at the previous review interval
answerChoices.rationale: The previous minimally disruptive symptom pattern no longer applies.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The previous minimally disruptive symptom pattern no longer applies.

answerChoices.label: Refer for emergency abdominal exploration today
answerChoices.rationale: The local pain resolves with reduction and no current obstruction or persistent tenderness is described.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The local pain resolves with reduction and no current obstruction or persistent tenderness is described.

questions.explanation: The new evidence is failure of ordinary work because of pain that tracks the protrusion and resolves with reduction. That supports elective repair evaluation. Reducibility alone does not justify continuing the old plan, and the current findings do not establish an emergency.

questions.stem: Which next plan best addresses Luis Carter's persistent lifting pain?

answerChoices.label: Refer for elective epigastric hernia repair assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The focal defect and reproducible reduction response identify a mechanical problem distinct from the improved core instability.

answerChoices.label: Extend the same core rehabilitation programme
answerChoices.rationale: Rehabilitation improved the broad functional complaint but has not addressed the focal reduction-responsive pain.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Rehabilitation improved the broad functional complaint but has not addressed the focal reduction-responsive pain.

answerChoices.label: Observe the focal defect at routine annual review
answerChoices.rationale: The specific ongoing task limitation warrants elective assessment rather than another incidental-defect review.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The specific ongoing task limitation warrants elective assessment rather than another incidental-defect review.

questions.explanation: Two problems can coexist. Improvement in balance does not explain away pain that is reproduced by protrusion through a focal defect and stops with reduction. That persistent mechanical symptom supports elective hernia assessment.

questions.stem: Which imaging plan best addresses the uncertainty in Nora Ellis's intermittent lateral lump?

answerChoices.label: Targeted ultrasound during upright straining
answerChoices.rationale: Reproduce the provoking conditions at the correct site to assess an intermittent defect missed at rest.

answerChoices.label: Repeat targeted ultrasound while supine at rest
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the same acquisition does not address why the protrusion was missed.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating the same acquisition does not address why the protrusion was missed.

answerChoices.label: Routine supine CT without a provoking manoeuvre
answerChoices.rationale: CT can diagnose this hernia, but repeating the resting condition is less directly suited to this small intermittent finding than targeted dynamic assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CT can diagnose this hernia, but repeating the resting condition is less directly suited to this small intermittent finding than targeted dynamic assessment.

questions.explanation: The negative study sampled the correct site in a state when the lump disappears. Dynamic targeted assessment addresses that limitation. CT remains a valid diagnostic route in appropriate cases; this item does not declare ultrasound universally superior.

questions.stem: Which plan best addresses Nora Ellis's returned abdominal-wall findings?

answerChoices.label: Elective surgical assessment for mesh repair
answerChoices.rationale: An interparietal lateral defect with meaningful symptoms warrants repair evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Physiotherapy for widened midline connective tissue
answerChoices.rationale: This is a focal lateral opening rather than an intact broad midline separation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a focal lateral opening rather than an intact broad midline separation.

answerChoices.label: Hospital admission for emergency exploration
answerChoices.rationale: The observed sac returns and there are no current obstructive or ischemic findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The observed sac returns and there are no current obstructive or ischemic findings.

questions.explanation: Infer a focal lateral interparietal hernia from the findings, then use its current symptoms and reducibility to choose the pathway. Elective mesh-repair assessment is appropriate. The evidence does not select one open or laparoscopic technique for every Spigelian hernia.

questions.stem: Which initial source-control plan best fits Daniel Brooks's recorded findings?

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous drainage with culture-directed antibiotics
answerChoices.rationale: This recently symptomatic stable localized extraperitoneal process can undergo a specialist-directed salvage attempt. The implant and course still require reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Complete mesh excision with operative debridement
answerChoices.rationale: Excision may become necessary, but the record does not yet show failed salvage or sepsis making this the preferred initial choice.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Excision may become necessary, but the record does not yet show failed salvage or sepsis making this the preferred initial choice.

answerChoices.label: Skin-tract debridement with local dressings
answerChoices.rationale: The cultured cavity lies at the implant plane; treating the exit does not control the deep focus.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The cultured cavity lies at the implant plane; treating the exit does not control the deep focus.

questions.explanation: A small skin opening can drain a deep prosthetic focus. Daniel's stability and localized findings permit a monitored salvage attempt using drainage and antibiotics, rather than surface care or automatic complete removal. The completed evaluation did not demonstrate a fistula; it does not guarantee one can never emerge.

questions.stem: Which source-control recommendation now best fits Daniel Brooks's persistent infection?

answerChoices.label: Excise mesh and debride the repair plane
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent microbiologically supported infection after adequate drainage and directed therapy raises a retained-prosthesis source-control problem.

answerChoices.label: Retain mesh and repeat drainage with directed antibiotics
answerChoices.rationale: The cavity was already drained and the regimen matched the organism, yet infection recurred at the implant.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The cavity was already drained and the regimen matched the organism, yet infection recurred at the implant.

answerChoices.label: Retain mesh and excise the cutaneous sinus tract
answerChoices.rationale: Closing or removing the tract alone leaves the documented deep infected focus.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Closing or removing the tract alone leaves the documented deep infected focus.

questions.explanation: A collapsed fluid cavity is not the same as eradication of implant infection. The documented drainage and culture-directed course were adequate, yet purulence and the same organism recurred at the retained mesh. Operative excision assessment is appropriate; the exact removal extent and reconstruction plan require the treating team.

questions.stem: Which recommendation should have guided Aisha Morgan's care at that recorded assessment?

answerChoices.label: Urgent operative source-control assessment with resuscitation
answerChoices.rationale: The matched deep/blood organisms and deteriorating physiology require hospital source control, including mesh excision assessment.

answerChoices.label: Outpatient drainage with a planned oral antibiotic course
answerChoices.rationale: A stable outpatient salvage pathway does not fit confusion and hypotension.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A stable outpatient salvage pathway does not fit confusion and hypotension.

answerChoices.label: Local wound debridement with routine clinic follow-up

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local skin treatment does not address the bloodstream and prosthetic-plane focus.

questions.explanation: Interpret both the source and the physiology. This was a deep prosthetic infection with systemic deterioration, requiring hospital resuscitation and urgent surgical source-control assessment. It was not a stable outpatient salvage situation.

questions.stem: Which plan best fits Helen Parker's findings at that recorded assessment?

answerChoices.label: Resuscitate and arrange emergency operative exploration
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent nonreducibility, guarding and reduced enhancement raise concern for compromised bowel; recent stool passage does not negate those findings.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeated reduction attempts are not the preferred path when ischemia is suspected.
